title: On Manhood
subtitle: Fatherhood, work, and being a man who stays
blurb: Essays on manhood from a man raised without a father and raising five sons — fatherhood, provision, anger, presence, and the men the church forgot to form.

chapters.title: Biblical Womanhood Beyond the Debate
chapters.summary: Complementarian and egalitarian Christians have fought over a handful of verses for decades. Both sides have something true and something to answer for. Here is the harder question underneath the debate.
chapters.body:
There is a debate that has consumed a great deal of energy in the American church for the last fifty years, and I want to walk into it carefully, because I have watched it wound people I love. It is the debate over what the Bible teaches about women, men, marriage, and the church. The two camps have names. Complementarian and egalitarian. Most Christians have never used either word out loud and yet have strong feelings about the thing the words describe. Let me try to state each position the way its own best defenders would state it, before I say anything else. If you can tell from my summary alone where I land, I have failed the first task.

The complementarian case, at its strongest

The complementarian argues that God created men and women equal in worth and dignity, both bearing his image (Genesis 1:27), and different in role, and that this difference is not a curse of the fall but a feature of the good creation before the fall. He points to the order of creation in Genesis 2, to which Paul appeals directly in 1 Timothy 2:13. He points to Ephesians 5, where the husband is called to a headship defined entirely by self-giving love, "as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25), a headship that looks like a cross and not a throne. He points to 1 Corinthians 11:3 and the ordering it describes, and to the pastoral qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1, which assume male elders.

The strongest version of this position, associated with scholars like Wayne Grudem and the late thoughtful pastor Tim Keller, is not about competence or capacity. It does not claim women are less intelligent, less gifted, or less spiritual. It claims that God has assigned distinct and complementary callings, that authority in the home and the ordained office of elder are given to qualified men, and that this is not a demotion of women any more than the Son's submission to the Father is a demotion of the Son within the equal Trinity. The best complementarians grieve the abuse done in the name of male headship and insist that a headship not spent in sacrifice is a counterfeit. They say the world's problem is not too much biblical masculinity but too little of the real thing.

Let me press their case even harder than they sometimes press it themselves, because a steelman that stops early is a straw man in better clothing. The complementarian can point out that the surrounding culture's account of equality has often meant sameness, an erasure of any given difference between men and women, and that this erasure has not obviously served women well. He can note that the therapeutic and consumer culture that promised women liberation through sameness has left a great many of them exhausted, and that the biblical vision of distinct and honored callings might be a mercy the culture cannot recognize. He can observe that the male headship the Bible describes is not the male dominance the world knows, that Ephesians 5 gives the husband no rights and only a costly duty, to love his wife as Christ loved the church and died for her, which is the most demanding assignment in the entire passage. The wife is asked to submit. The husband is asked to die. If you are keeping score of who got the harder command, the complementarian will tell you it was the man, and the honest reader has to concede he has a point about the text.

The egalitarian case, at its strongest

The egalitarian argues that the same Bible, read whole, points toward the full and equal participation of women in every sphere including church leadership. She points to Genesis 1, where both male and female are given dominion together with no hierarchy named. She argues that the subordination of woman to man in Genesis 3:16, "your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you," is described as a consequence of the fall, part of the brokenness Christ came to reverse, not a creation ordinance to preserve.

She points to Galatians 3:28, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus," and argues that if we rightly read the slave and free clause as undoing an entire social hierarchy, we should read the male and female clause the same way. She points to the women I named earlier, Deborah judging, Huldah authenticating, Phoebe carrying Romans, Junia the apostle, Priscilla teaching Apollos. She reads the restrictive passages, 1 Timothy 2 and 1 Corinthians 14, as addressed to specific first-century situations, disorder in the Corinthian assembly, false teaching spreading through the Ephesian church, rather than as timeless prohibitions. The New Testament scholars Gordon Fee and Ben Witherington and, on the theological side, the late thoughtful writer scholars associated with the group Christians for Biblical Equality have made this case with rigor. The best egalitarians are not importing a secular agenda. They are asking the church to be more biblical, not less, by attending to the whole witness of Scripture rather than a favored shelf of it.

And here too let me press the case past where its advocates sometimes leave it. The egalitarian can point out that the same interpretive move used to keep women from the pulpit, reading a first-century instruction as a timeless creation ordinance, was once used with equal confidence to keep slaves in their place, since Paul told slaves to obey their masters and grounded it in the household order of his day. The church eventually learned to read those texts as bound to a social world Christ was quietly undoing rather than sanctioning forever. The egalitarian asks, with real force, why the male and female clause of Galatians 3:28 should be treated differently from the slave and free clause sitting right beside it in the same sentence. She can note that the trajectory of Scripture, from the shared dominion of Genesis 1 through the reversal of the curse in Christ to the outpouring of the prophetic Spirit on daughters at Pentecost, bends toward inclusion, and that a faithful reading attends not only to isolated verses but to the direction the whole story is traveling. This is not the culture talking. This is a serious argument from the shape of redemption, and the honest complementarian has to answer it rather than dismiss it.

Naming the order of the question

Before I go further I owe you honesty about how much this question weighs. The historic creeds, Nicaea and Chalcedon, do not settle it. The Apostles' Creed does not settle it. This is not a first-order question on the level of the Trinity or the bodily resurrection of Christ, where the faith itself is at stake. It is a second-order question, one over which faithful churches divide and have divided for a very long time without either side ceasing to be the church. That matters enormously for how we treat each other in it. A person who lands differently than you on the ordination of women is not thereby a heretic, and the moment we speak as though they are, we have inflated a second-order question into a first-order one, which is its own kind of error.

I hold a view. I am not going to pretend I do not, and it would be cowardice to hide behind a false neutrality. But I am going to hold it in front of you in a way that keeps a brother or sister on the other side reading, because if I cannot do that, my view is not worth much.

Where I land, and the objection I have not fully answered

I find myself persuaded that the restrictive texts are more situationally bound than the tradition I was raised in allowed, and that the sweep of Scripture, the prophetesses, the apostle Junia, the deacon Phoebe, the reversal Christ works on the curse, leans toward a fuller participation of women than most of my churches practiced. That is where I land, and it comes from the broadly egalitarian tradition, though I hold it without contempt for the other side.

Here is the strongest objection I have not fully answered, and I will not pretend I have. Paul grounds his instruction in 1 Timothy 2 not in the local situation but in the creation order itself: "For Adam was formed first, then Eve" (1 Timothy 2:13). That is not a cultural argument. That is an appeal to something before the fall, before culture. The honest egalitarian has to do real work with that verse, and the honest complementarian is right to press it. I do that work, and I find the reading available, but I will not tell you it is effortless or that the complementarian is a fool for weighing that verse more heavily than I do. He is weighing a real thing.

The harder question underneath

Now I want to say the thing that the whole debate has been distracting us from. Both camps have been so busy fighting over who can stand behind a pulpit that we have largely ignored a prior and heavier question. What is the church for? And what is a human being for?

The debate over roles assumes we already know what leadership is, what authority is, what a good life is, and we are only arguing about who gets to have it. But the New Testament keeps refusing that assumption. When the disciples argued about who was the greatest, Jesus did not adjudicate the argument. He overturned the table it was sitting on. "Whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all" (Mark 10:43 to 44). The kingdom does not run on the logic of who gets the authority. It runs on the logic of who spends themselves last.

I have watched complementarian men use headship as a warrant for control, which is the exact opposite of the cross-shaped headship their own best theologians describe, and I have watched egalitarian churches chase the culture's account of power so closely that they forgot the cross-shaped part entirely, treating leadership as a prize to be distributed fairly rather than a burden to be carried sacrificially. Both errors share a root. Both have accepted the world's definition of what authority is and only argued about its allotment.

What my own house taught me

I have five sons. I did not have a father in my own house growing up, and so I have had to learn fatherhood from scratch, without a template, in real time, in front of them. And the thing I have learned, slowly and often too late, is that the authority that actually forms a child is almost never the authority that announces itself. It is the authority of the parent who is up at three in the morning, who apologizes first, who is present when it costs something. My sons have never once obeyed me because I cited a verse about my position. They have followed me, when they have followed me at all, because they watched me stay.

That has quietly reordered how I read the whole debate. The question the New Testament is pressing on both camps is not chiefly who is in charge. It is whether anyone in charge is willing to be poured out. And on that question, the honest complementarian and the honest egalitarian are closer to each other than either is to the surrounding culture, which believes that power is for having and keeping.

The sociologist Christian Smith, in his 2005 study Soul Searching, gave a name to the actual folk religion of much of American church life, moralistic therapeutic deism, a faith in which God exists mainly to make us feel good about ourselves and to solve our problems on request. I raise it here because I have come to think the roles debate often runs on that unexamined substrate. Both sides, at their weakest, argue about women's roles as though the point of the church were the flourishing and self-actualization of its members, with the only question being how to distribute the opportunities fairly or how to protect a divine order that guarantees them. But the church does not exist to actualize anyone. It exists to form a people who look like the crucified Christ. The moment the debate becomes a fight over who gets to flourish in which role, it has already accepted a therapeutic account of the church that neither Paul nor Jesus would recognize, and both camps have breathed it in without noticing.

The test

So here is my test, and I hold it against myself first. If a woman who has landed on the other side of this question from me reads what I have written and feels beaten rather than understood, I have failed, no matter how right my exegesis. And if the debate over women's roles has made either camp more certain of its tribe and less able to see the cruciform pattern that judges every account of authority, then the debate has cost us more than it has taught us.

The church did not need another position on women. It needed to become a place where the last are actually first, where authority looks like a basin and a towel, where the daughters in the pews are formed by watching sacrifice and not by hearing arguments. We have given them the arguments. We owe them the sacrifice. Until we pay it, the debate is just noise we make while the actual work goes undone.

chapters.title: Fatherhood Without a Father: Breaking the Cycle
chapters.summary: I had no template. When my first son was born, I stood in the hospital holding a person I was responsible for, and I did not have a single memory of being fathered to draw on.
chapters.body:
I had no template. When my first son was born, I stood in the hospital holding a person I was responsible for, and I did not have a single memory of being fathered to draw on. Other men, I imagined, had a voice in their head, their own father's voice, this is how you hold him, this is what you say, this is what a father does here. I had silence. Where the template should have been, there was an absence, and I was expected to build a father out of nothing while a newborn depended on me getting it right.

I grew up without a father. I have written about coming to faith from atheism, about being raised by a mother doing the work of two, about the particular ache of a boy who does not have a man in the house to show him what a man is. And I have five sons now. Which means the question of whether a fatherless boy can become a father is not academic to me. It is the central experiment of my adult life, still running, still uncertain, and I am inside it.

The Absence That Speaks

People assume that growing up without a father means you learned nothing about fathering. It is worse than that. You learned a great deal. You learned it from the absence, and absence is a loud teacher. The lesson a fatherless boy absorbs, whether or not he can articulate it, is that fathers leave, or fathers fail, or fathers are simply not there when a boy needs them, and that a man handles his own pain alone because there was no one to hand it to.

An absent father does not fail to teach. He teaches absence. He teaches that men disappear. And the fatherless boy carries that curriculum into his own fatherhood, where it waits to be repeated unless something interrupts it.

The interruption is the whole game. Because the default, the path of least resistance, is repetition. The abused become abusers, the abandoned abandon, the sons of absent fathers grow into absent fathers, not because they want to but because the groove is worn deep and water runs downhill. The cycle is not a metaphor. It is a measurable pattern, generation after generation, and every man who breaks it is fighting gravity. I did not want to repeat my father. Wanting is not enough. Plenty of men who swore they would never become their fathers became them anyway, because you cannot defeat a pattern you have not examined, and the pattern operates below the level of intention.

The specific way the absence taught me was subtle, and I did not see it operating until I caught myself doing it. When my sons pushed against me, when there was conflict, my first instinct was not to engage but to withdraw, to go cold and quiet and distant, to remove my presence as a form of self-protection. That was the absence, reproducing itself. My father handled a difficult relationship by not being in it, and when things got difficult with my own sons, my body reached, without my permission, for the same solution. Absence is not only a thing that happens to you. It is a thing you learn to do, and it comes back most strongly in exactly the moments a child needs you to stay.

You Cannot Give What You Did Not Receive, and Yet

There is a truth in the saying that you cannot give what you did not receive, and there is a lie in it, and the fatherless father has to sort them out or be destroyed by the confusion. The truth is that I do not have an instinctive, embodied knowledge of fathering, the kind that a well-fathered man carries in his hands without thinking. I have to do consciously what other men do automatically. Every warm gesture toward my sons was, at first, a decision rather than a reflex, because the reflex was not installed.

The lie is that this means I am doomed to fail them. Because a thing that is missing can be sought. What is not given by inheritance can be gained by grace, by observation, by desperate attention, by the deliberate acquisition of a fathering I never received. I have watched other fathers the way an immigrant studies a new language, taking notes, trying phrases, failing, adjusting. I have read, prayed, asked, apologized, and started over. It is exhausting in a way that well-fathered men do not understand, because for them it is native and for me it is a second language I am still learning to speak without an accent. But a second language can be learned. Fluency is possible. It just costs more.

And there is a strange gift buried in the deficit, which I did not see for years. The well-fathered man often fathers on autopilot, reproducing what he received without ever examining it, which means he passes on the flaws along with the strengths, unconsciously, because it never occurs to him to question a pattern that feels like water to a fish. The fatherless man cannot father on autopilot, because there is no autopilot to run. Everything is a choice. And a man who has to choose every gesture is, at least, capable of choosing well, of examining each pattern before he passes it on, of building deliberately rather than inheriting blindly. The deficit forces an intentionality that the inheritance never requires. It is a terrible way to acquire the gift. But it is a way, and the gift is real.

The Father I Found

I came to faith as an adult, out of atheism, and I want to be honest about what that meant for the fatherless part of me, because it is easy to make this too neat and I distrust neatness. When I encountered the God the Bible calls Father, I did not feel an instant healing of the father-wound. That is the testimony people want, and it is usually not true. What I found was slower and stranger. I found a category I had never been able to fill, Father, and a Person offering to fill it, and a lifetime of learning to let him.

The gospel did not hand me a father the way you hand someone a package. It handed me a Father the way you hand someone a marriage, an unfinished relationship that has to be lived into over decades, where the wounds surface and get healed and surface again.

What this gave me, practically, was a template after all. Not from my own childhood, but from watching how God fathers. He does not disappear. He disciplines without crushing. He runs toward the son who wasted everything, while the son is still far off, and does not make him grovel. He is present in the ordinary and present in the catastrophe. Slowly, I began to father my sons out of that template, the one I received late, from God, rather than the one I never received from my father. I was learning to be a dad by learning to have one. The order surprised me. It should not have.

The parable of the prodigal son did particular work in me, because it is a portrait of a father doing the exact opposite of what my instincts told me a father does. The son insults him, leaves, wastes everything, and comes back, and the father, who had every right to make him earn his way home, runs. He runs to a son who does not deserve it, and embraces him before the apology is finished, and throws a party. My instinct, the instinct absence taught me, was to make a returning son prove himself, to hold him at a distance until he had earned re-entry. The parable told me that this instinct was not fatherhood. It was the wound talking. Real fatherhood runs.

What Breaking the Cycle Actually Requires

Breaking the cycle is not a moment of decision. It is a thousand small refusals, repeated over years, each one against the grain. The moment my son does something that triggers the old inheritance, the flash of rage, the impulse to withdraw, the urge to handle my hurt by going silent and cold the way absence taught me, and I feel the groove pulling me down it, and I choose, in that specific instant, to do the other thing. To stay. To speak. To move toward him instead of away. Each of those refusals is small. There are ten thousand of them. Together they are the cycle breaking, one instant at a time.

It requires knowing your triggers, which requires examining the very wounds you would rather leave buried. The fatherless man who refuses to look at his father-wound will father from it blindly. The one who does the painful excavation, in therapy, in prayer, in honest conversation with someone safe, gains the ability to see the pattern coming and step out of its path. You cannot dodge what you cannot see. Self-knowledge, for the fatherless father, is not navel-gazing. It is armor for his children. Every hour I have spent understanding what my father's absence did to me is an hour that protected my sons from inheriting it unexamined.

The Grief You Have to Feel to Get Free

Here is the part men skip, and skipping it is why so many of them stay stuck. To break the cycle, you have to grieve the father you did not have. Not intellectually acknowledge it. Grieve it. Feel the loss of the thing every child deserves and you did not get. Most fatherless men have wrapped that grief in a hard shell of I turned out fine and I did not need him anyway, and the shell is a lie, and until it cracks, the unfelt grief leaks out sideways into the next generation.

I had to sit with the fact that I was robbed. That a boy who deserved a father did not get one, and that boy was me, and it was not fair, and it left a mark that has shaped my whole life. Feeling that, actually feeling it rather than managing it, was the thing that freed me to father my sons without secretly resenting them for having what I did not, and without unconsciously reenacting on them the abandonment I suffered. The unmourned wound gets passed on. The mourned wound gets transformed into wisdom. Grief is not weakness for the fatherless man. It is the doorway out of the cycle, and it is the door most men refuse to walk through because it hurts, and so they stay, and so do their sons.

Fathering the Boy You Were

Something happens when a fatherless man fathers well. He fathers his sons, yes. But he also, in some real sense, fathers the boy he used to be. Every time I show up for my sons in a way no one showed up for me, I am giving to them what I never got, and I am also, obliquely, healing the place in me where that gift should have gone. It is not a substitute for the healing God does. It is part of it. The giving heals the giver. The father-wound closes a little more each time I refuse to reopen it in my children.

This is why I do not believe the fatherless are cursed to repeat the pattern, though I understand why they fear it, because I feared it, because the fear was rational. The pattern is powerful. It is not destiny. Grace interrupts it. Examination interrupts it. A found Father interrupts it. Ten thousand small refusals interrupt it. And a man who was raised without a father can, against every odd, become the father his own father was not, and in doing so bend the whole line of his family in a new direction that his grandsons will inherit without ever knowing what it cost him.

The Uncertain Ending, Because It Is Honest

I will not tell you I have broken the cycle cleanly, because I do not know yet, and the men who claim total victory make me nervous. My sons are still becoming who they will be. Some of the marks of my fatherlessness surely made it into them despite everything, in ways I cannot see and they have not yet named. The experiment is still running. I will not have the results in my lifetime. The real verdict comes when my sons father their sons, and I may not be here for it.

What I know is this. I did not repeat my father's absence. I was present. I stayed. I did the excavation, felt the grief, found a Father, and made the ten thousand small refusals, and I am still making them. Whether that is enough, my grandsons will tell my sons, in ways none of us can predict. But the cycle that ran unbroken through the men before me hit, in me, an interruption. Not a clean break. An interruption. And sometimes an interruption is all grace needs. It is what I had. It is what I gave. It will have to be enough, and I have to trust the God who fathered me late to finish in my sons what I could only begin.

chapters.title: Fatherhood: The Most Overlooked Ministry
chapters.summary: We celebrate the men who plant churches and cross oceans, and we say almost nothing to the man who is quietly shaping eternal souls at his own breakfast table.
chapters.body:
There is a strange silence in the church about the most consequential thing most men will ever do. We will spend a Sunday celebrating the missionary who spent two years in a difficult country. We will honor the man who left his career to plant a church. We will build entire services around vocational calling and radical obedience. And we will say almost nothing, from any pulpit, to the man sitting in the fourth row who is shaping five human souls at his kitchen table every single morning and has no idea that he is doing ministry at all.

I want to argue that fatherhood is not a lesser calling that some men happen to have alongside their real work. For most of the men reading this, fatherhood is the real work. It is the most sustained, most intimate, most eternally significant ministry they will ever be given, and the church has largely failed to tell them so.

The ministry no one applauds

Part of the reason we overlook it is that fatherhood produces no measurable numbers. A pastor can report baptisms. A missionary can report converts. A conference speaker can report attendance. But what does a father report. That he was patient at dinner. That he did not lose his temper in the car. That he prayed with a frightened child at two in the morning and forgot it by breakfast. None of this shows up on a spreadsheet. None of it will be mentioned from a stage. And so the man begins to believe, without anyone ever saying it directly, that this part of his life is not really the important part. The important part is out there, where the applause is.

This is a lie, and it is a lie with a very long tail. Because the father who believes it will pour himself into the arenas that reward him and give his children the exhausted remnant. He will be present at the church and absent at home. He will disciple other people's teenagers and be a stranger to his own. And he will do all of it with a clear conscience, because everyone around him is telling him that his kingdom work is what happens under a steeple, not what happens under his own roof.

A man will be tempted to give his best hours to the place that applauds him and his leftover hours to the people who need him most.

What a father actually transmits

Consider what is really being handed down at that breakfast table. A child does not learn who God is primarily from a sermon. A child learns who God is from a father, long before the child has language for it. Every time a father is faithful, the child's imagination of a faithful God is quietly built. Every time a father is absent, or cruel, or distracted, or unpredictable, that too is being written into the child's picture of the divine, in a place too deep for later argument to reach.

This is a terrifying thing to say out loud, and I say it as a man who has failed at it. My children's earliest and most durable sense of what a father is, they got from me, not from a book. When they hear that God is a Father, they will not run that word through a dictionary. They will run it through me. If I was harsh, God will feel harsh until grace does surgery on the memory. If I was distant, God will feel distant. If I was safe, they will have a head start on trusting a God they cannot see.

No missionary carries a weight like this. The missionary influences strangers for a season. The father shapes the deepest instincts of a soul that will exist forever, in the years when the clay is softest and the hands leave the deepest prints. If we understood this, we would treat the ordinary father with the reverence we reserve for the ordained.

The ministry of showing up

Let me be concrete, because I distrust sermons on fatherhood that stay in the clouds. The ministry of a father is not mostly made of the big moments. It is not the annual trip or the perfect Christmas or the one profound conversation. Those are real, but they are the exceptions, and children know it. What forms them is the accumulation, the ten thousand small hours.

It is the fact that you were there at pickup. That you knew the name of the friend and the name of the teacher and the name of the thing they were afraid of. That you noticed when they came home different and asked about it instead of turning on the television. That you were, above all, predictable, in the good sense, so that a child could build a life on the assumption that Dad would be where Dad said he would be. Presence is not glamorous. It cannot be photographed. But it is the raw material of everything.

Children do not remember the days you gave them. They remember that you were the kind of man who gave them the days.

I have watched men grasp this too late. Men whose children are grown and gone, who suddenly realize that the years they thought were preliminary were in fact the whole thing. That the career they were building toward some future season of presence was the very thing that stole the season from them. The season never comes later. There is no later. The children get older on schedule whether the father is watching or not.

The father as pastor of a small church

The most useful reframe I can offer a father is this. You are the pastor of a very small church. Your household is a congregation of a few souls, and you have been given spiritual authority over them, and you will give an account for how you shepherded them. This is not a metaphor to inflate the ordinary. It is a description of the actual structure the Scriptures assume. When Paul lists the qualifications for an elder, he asks whether the man manages his own household well, because the home is the training ground and the test of every other kind of leadership.

So think of your family as a flock. What does the pastor of a small church do. He teaches. He prays for his people by name. He knows their struggles. He is present in their crises. He models repentance when he fails them. He does not pretend to a perfection they can see through. He points them, again and again, past himself to the God he serves. Every one of these is available to you at your own table, tonight, without a title or a seminary degree or anyone's permission.

And here is the sobering symmetry. A man can be a competent pastor of a large church and a negligent pastor of the small one at home, and the Scripture is clear about which failure disqualifies him. We have it backward. We honor the man who succeeds publicly and shrug at his private neglect. God asks about the household first.

The discipleship that happens in the ordinary

Let me press further on what this ministry actually consists of, because I fear that even calling fatherhood a ministry can inflate it into something ceremonial, something a man does at set times with a Bible open. That is a small part of it, and not the largest. The formation of a child happens mostly in the unscheduled hours, in the car and at the sink and in the moments of interruption that a busy man is tempted to treat as obstacles to his real work. Those interruptions are the real work.

A father disciples his children not primarily through the family devotional, valuable as that may be, but through ten thousand ordinary responses to ordinary situations. How he reacts when the milk is spilled. Whether he tells the truth when a small lie would be easier. How he speaks about the neighbor he dislikes, the boss who treated him unfairly, the driver who cut him off. His children are watching all of it, absorbing a theology of daily life that no formal lesson could ever install, learning what it looks like to be a person who believes what this family claims to believe. The catechism is real, but the deeper catechism is the father's character under pressure, observed daily, unedited.

This is why fatherhood is such a searching ministry. It cannot be performed. A man can prepare a sermon and deliver a version of himself for forty minutes. He cannot prepare his whole life, and his children see the whole life, the unprepared parts most of all. They see him tired, they see him frightened about money, they see him at his least impressive, and they are forming their picture of God out of exactly those moments. The ministry of fatherhood is the ministry of being watched at your worst by the people whose souls you most want to protect, which is why it drives a man to grace faster than almost anything else. He cannot fake his way through it. He can only be honest, repent when he fails, and trust that God works even through a flawed father who is trying.

A word to the men who feel too late

Some men reading this are already grieving. The children are older, the pattern is set, the distance is real, and the temptation is to conclude that the ministry was missed and cannot be recovered. I want to speak against that despair, gently and firmly.

The ministry of fatherhood does not end when the children grow up. It changes shape. An adult child can still receive a father's repentance. A father can still, at sixty, go to a thirty year old son and name specifically the ways he failed him and ask his forgiveness, and something can be healed that no amount of earlier presence would have healed as deeply. It is never too late to become the father God is calling you to be, because the God who calls is a Father who restores the years the locusts have eaten.

The long view of a father's work

There is a temptation, in the middle of the exhausting years, to measure fatherhood by the day and to despair. A father comes to the end of a long day, having lost his patience twice and connected meaningfully with no one, and he concludes he is failing. But fatherhood is not measured by the day. It is measured by the decade, and by the direction of a life, and by the accumulation of ordinary faithfulness across years that no single day can reveal. The father who shows up, again and again, imperfectly, is building something that will not be visible for a very long time.

I have found it steadying to remember that God himself works this way with us, as a Father whose formation of his children unfolds across a whole life and is rarely visible in any given season. He is patient with the slow work, unbothered by the days that seem to accomplish nothing, faithful across the long arc when the results cannot yet be seen. A human father is invited into that same patience with his own children, released from the tyranny of measuring today and freed to trust the long work of a lifetime of presence. The seeds a father plants in a small child may not visibly grow for twenty years, and some of the most important ones will only bear their fruit after the father is gone.

Fatherhood is not measured by any single day. It is measured by the direction of a life, and most of its fruit ripens after the father can no longer see it.

It also helps to remember that our children do not need a perfect father, and in fact would not know what to do with one. A flawless father would give a child no template for grace, no picture of failure and repair, no model of how a good man handles his own wrongdoing. What our children need is a present father who is honest about his failures and faithful across the long arc, and that kind of father, imperfect and repentant and there, is available to any man willing to keep showing up. The pursuit of the perfect fatherhood is itself a trap, because it can drive a man to despair over the failures that were always going to happen, when what his children actually needed was not his perfection but his presence and his honesty about its absence.

So the father who feels he is failing on a particular Tuesday should take heart. The ministry is not the flawless day. The ministry is the faithful direction, held across years, through the failures and the repentances and the ordinary unremarkable presence that a child absorbs without either of them noticing. That is a ministry no applause will ever reach, and it is among the most important work being done anywhere on earth, and the God who assigned it is watching it with a father's own attention, and he does not overlook what the church so often does.

But do not use grace as an excuse to keep waiting. If your children are still in the house, the hour is now, and it is short, and it is holy. Put down the thing that has your best hours. Look at the small congregation God has entrusted to you. Learn their names again. This is not a distraction from your ministry. For most of you, this is your ministry, and it always was, and heaven has been watching it all along even when the church was looking somewhere else.

chapters.title: Female Friendship: The Relationships That Sustain You
chapters.summary: The church has praised marriage, honored motherhood, and left the friendships between women almost entirely undescribed. Scripture takes them more seriously than we do.
chapters.body:
I have five sons and no daughters, and one consequence of that arithmetic is that I have spent very little of my life inside the world of women's friendships. I have watched it from the edges. I have watched my wife on the phone with a friend for two hours after a hard week and get up from the couch a different person than she sat down. I have seen a woman in my congregation held together, quite literally, by three other women in a season when nothing else was holding. And I have noticed something that took me too long to notice: the church has almost nothing to say about it.

We have shelves of books on marriage. We have ministries for mothers. We have discipleship programs and small groups. But the friendship between two women, the thing that in my observation actually carries many of them through the years the marriage books never mention, is nearly absent from our teaching. We praise the covenant relationships and leave the sustaining ones undescribed. That is a strange omission for a book that opens its account of human need not with a spouse but with the plain observation that it is not good for a person to be alone.

The friendship the Bible chose to canonize

If you want to know how seriously Scripture takes friendship, notice which one it made a whole book out of. The book of Ruth is not, at its center, a romance. The romance with Boaz is the resolution. The engine of the story is the loyalty between two women, Naomi and Ruth, a widowed mother-in-law and a foreign daughter-in-law who owed her nothing.

Ruth's speech to Naomi in the first chapter is one of the most quoted passages at weddings, which is a small irony, because it was not spoken to a husband. It was spoken by one woman to another. "Where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried" (Ruth 1:16-17). That is covenant language. It is the language of a binding, self-giving loyalty, and Ruth aims it at a bitter old woman who has just told her to go home. The Bible looked at the relationship between two women in grief and said: this is worth a book. This is worth putting in the line of the Messiah, because Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of David and stands in the genealogy of Christ. The friendship is not a footnote to the story. It is the story.

We read Ruth's vow at weddings and forget she spoke it to a woman who had nothing to offer her. Which means we have heard the most famous words about loyalty in the Bible and missed who they were for.

What was lost when friendship became sentiment

To feel how thin our idea of friendship has become, it helps to know it was once thicker. The ancient world took friendship with a seriousness we have lost. Aristotle devoted two of the ten books of his Nicomachean Ethics to it and distinguished three kinds: friendships of utility, friendships of pleasure, and the friendship of virtue, in which two people love each other for the sake of the good and become better through the loving. That third kind, Aristotle said, was rare and slow and the closest thing to the good life a human could have.

The Christian tradition inherited this and deepened it. In the twelfth century, a Cistercian abbot named Aelred of Rievaulx wrote a whole treatise called Spiritual Friendship, arguing that friendship between believers is a place where the love of God is made concrete, that "a friend is the medicine of life," and that to move from friendship to the friendship of Christ is a natural ascent. Aelred was not talking about acquaintances. He was talking about the kind of bond in which two souls are so joined that they can bear each other's burdens and speak each other's sins and still remain.

Something happened to that idea, and I think we can date it roughly. As romantic marriage rose in the modern West to absorb all the weight of human intimacy, friendship deflated. C.S. Lewis, in The Four Loves (1960), diagnosed it precisely. Friendship, he wrote, is the least natural of the loves, the least instinctive, the least necessary to survival and reproduction, and for exactly that reason the modern world, obsessed with what is natural and necessary, cannot see it. "To the ancients, Friendship seemed the happiest and most fully human of all loves; the crown of life and the school of virtue. The modern world, in comparison, ignores it." Lewis said the modern world barely believes friendship is a real love at all. We have not disproven him.

What women's friendship carries that marriage cannot

Here I have to speak as an observer rather than an insider, and I will try to do it without pretending to know from the inside what I only know from the edge.

What I have watched, over fifteen years of pastoring, is that the friendships between women carry a specific weight that marriage is not designed to carry and often cannot. A wife cannot be her husband's only interpreter of her own experience, because he does not share it. My wife's friends understand things about her life, her body, her fears, her exhaustion, that I structurally cannot understand no matter how much I love her. When she comes home from a friend, she has been known in a register I do not have access to. That is not a threat to our marriage. It is a gift to it. A wife whose only intimacy is her husband is a wife with too much weight on one relationship, and I have seen that weight crush marriages that could have survived if the woman had not been so alone.

The friendships also do something marriages are not built to do: they witness a whole life. A husband arrives partway through the story. A friend of thirty years remembers who you were at twenty, holds the earlier selves you have half-forgotten, and can tell you when you are drifting from the person you meant to become. That kind of long witness is a form of accountability the culture has almost entirely lost, and it is one of the reasons the older women in Titus 2:3-5 are told to teach the younger. The mechanism of that teaching is not a classroom. It is friendship across the generations, the older woman who has walked the road speaking to the younger one who is on it.

The friendship that also has to be able to wound

There is a strand in Scripture on friendship that the sentimental version leaves out entirely, and it is the strand that separates real friendship from mere companionship. A real friend can hurt you on purpose, for your good, and a companion who only ever soothes is not the deeper thing. "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy" (Proverbs 27:6). And a few verses on: "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another" (Proverbs 27:17). Iron sharpening iron is not a gentle image. It is friction, sparks, the grinding of one hard thing against another until an edge appears. The friendship that only comforts and never corrects is missing half of what the book of Proverbs thinks friendship is for.

I raise this because women's friendships, for all their depth, face a particular temptation, which is the temptation to make loyalty mean agreement. To be a good friend can quietly come to mean always taking her side, always affirming, never being the one who says the hard true thing about the man she is dating or the choice she is making or the grudge she is nursing. That is not friendship at its fullest. That is a mutual non-aggression pact dressed as intimacy. The friend who will tell you that you are wrong, who will risk the friendship to say what needs saying, is rarer and more valuable than the friend who only ever agrees, and the difference between them is the difference between iron and cotton.

The reason this matters theologically is that God himself is described as a friend who wounds. "The Lord your God is in your midst," Zephaniah says, and the same God who "will rejoice over you with gladness" is the God who disciplines those he loves (Zephaniah 3:17; Hebrews 12:6). The friendship of God is not flattery. Jesus called his disciples friends, "for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you" (John 15:15), and what he made known to them included their coming failures, their pride, their need. The model of divine friendship is a candor that costs something. A women's friendship that has grown into that kind of candor, that can bear a hard word and survive it, is a stronger and holier thing than one that has stayed comfortable. Comfort is not the goal. It is a byproduct of a bond secure enough to tell the truth.

Why the church should build for it

Let me name what I think we have gotten wrong, and let me implicate myself first, because I have designed church programs for years and I have almost never designed for this.

Our default church structures are built around the family unit and the affinity group. We gather people who are alike, young marrieds with young marrieds, moms with moms, and we call it fellowship. But the friendships that actually sustain women often cut across the categories we sort them into, and they take a kind of time and depth that a weekly small group with a curriculum does not produce. Real friendship is slow. It is inefficient. It cannot be programmed, only made room for. And the modern church, optimized for attendance and engagement, is not good at making room for slow, unproductive, deep human bonds. We are good at events. We are bad at friendship. I have run the events.

The correction is not another program, which would miss the point entirely. It is a change of imagination. It is recognizing that when a woman is drowning, the thing that most often saves her is not the pastor and not the marriage seminar but two or three friends who will not leave. It is building a church culture that honors those friendships out loud, that names them from the pulpit as a form of the love of God, that treats a woman's deep friendships not as a private matter beside her real spiritual life but as part of it.

The weight this leaves

I said I watch this from the edge, and I do. But there is one thing I have seen clearly enough to stake a claim on.

At the funerals I have officiated for women, the marriage is honored, and the children speak, and those things are right and good. But over and over, the person who cannot get through the eulogy, the one whose grief is a different kind, is the friend of forty years. The one who was there before the husband and after the children left. The one who knew. Scripture put a friendship at the head of the line of David and called it worthy of a book. The church, for all its talk of relationship, has never quite believed how much a friend can carry.

And there is a warning folded into all of this for the church that means to take friendship seriously. Friendship cannot be manufactured, but it can be starved, and the modern church has a genius for starving it. A congregation that fills every night of the week with programs, that measures its health by the busyness of its calendar, leaves no room for the slow, unscheduled, unproductive hours in which real friendship is made. Friendship grows in margin, in the leftover time, in the meal that runs long because nobody had to be anywhere. A church can crowd it out with good things and never notice the loss, because the loss does not show up on any attendance sheet. It shows up years later, in the woman who is surrounded by a busy congregation and has no one to call at midnight. The remedy is not another initiative but a strange kind of restraint, the willingness to leave a night empty so that people have time to become something to one another. A church that guards margin the way it guards its programs would be doing more for the friendships of its women than any curriculum could, and it would cost nothing but the courage to do less. That courage is rarer among pastors than it should be, and I include myself in the shortage, because an empty night on the calendar feels like a failure of ministry rather than a gift of it, and I have filled far too many of them with things that mattered less than the friendships they crowded out.

The women in your congregation who are still standing after everything are usually standing on the shoulders of a friend you have never thought to thank. It is not good for a person to be alone. God said that first, before the marriages, before the children, before any of it. We keep forgetting what he meant.

chapters.title: Male Friendship Crisis
chapters.summary: A generation of men has drifted into a quiet isolation they cannot name, surrounded by acquaintances and starving for a friend. The consequences are showing up everywhere but the one place we look.
chapters.body:
Ask a middle aged man how many close friends he has, friends he could call at two in the morning in the worst hour of his life, and watch his face. Often he has never been asked, and he has to think about it, and the thinking takes longer than it should, and the answer that comes back is a number close to zero. He has coworkers. He has guys he watches the game with. He has the fathers of his children's friends and the men at his church whom he greets warmly by name. What he does not have is a friend. And until you asked, he had not fully noticed.

This is one of the quietest crises of our time, and it is quiet precisely because the men suffering from it have no framework for naming it. A man knows when he is unemployed. A man knows when his marriage is failing. But the slow disappearance of friendship happens without any single event, and so it registers not as a loss but as a vague low grade loneliness that the man assumes is simply what adulthood feels like. It is not what adulthood must feel like. It is what male adulthood has come to feel like because of specific things that happened, and things that happen can be reversed.

How the friendships disappeared

It helps to see how a man arrives here, because it is rarely a choice and usually a drift. In childhood and youth, friendship was effortless and constant, because proximity was constant. You saw the same boys every day, for years, with nothing to do but be together. Friendship in those years required no scheduling and no vulnerability, only presence, and presence was automatic.

Then the structures that provided automatic presence fell away one by one. School ended. The men scattered to cities and careers. Marriage came, and rightly reordered a man's priorities, but often absorbed the entire remainder of his relational energy, so that his wife became not only his spouse but his sole confidant, his only friend, the one person who knew anything true about him. Children came and consumed what was left. And through all of it, no one ever told the man that friendship, which had been free his whole young life, would now cost effort, would now require scheduling and initiative and a willingness to be the one who reaches out. So he did not pay the cost, because he did not know there was one, and the friendships quietly starved.

No one warned us that after a certain age, friendship stops being free. It now costs effort, and the men who will not pay it go without.

The wife who became the only friend

I want to name a specific pattern, because it is common and it is costly to a marriage in a way most couples never diagnose. Many men make their wives their only real relationship. She is the sole person who knows their fears, their struggles, their interior. On the surface this looks like intimacy, and a husband may even be proud of it, thinking it a sign of a close marriage.

But it is a crushing weight to place on one person. A wife was never meant to be a man's entire relational world. When she is his only friend, then every ordinary marital conflict becomes existential, because she is not just his spouse in that moment, she is his only human connection, and to be at odds with her is to be utterly alone. He has no other well to draw from. He has no other man who knows him and can steady him and tell him he is being a fool with love. So he clings, or he explodes, and either way the marriage groans under a load it was not built to bear. A man with real friendships is a better husband, because he is not asking his wife to be everyone.

Why men will not reach out

So why do men not simply fix this, if the diagnosis is this clear. Because reaching out requires the two things men have been most thoroughly trained to avoid. It requires initiative in the face of possible rejection, and it requires admitting need. To call another man and say, in effect, I would like to be your friend, I have been lonely, can we spend time together, feels to most men like an unbearable exposure. It sounds needy. It sounds like something a man should not have to say. And so no one says it, and every man waits for another man to go first, and they all sit in their separate houses assuming the loneliness is theirs alone.

Every man is waiting for another man to admit he is lonely first. So they all wait, and they all stay alone, and they all assume they are the only one.

The tragedy is that the exposure is imaginary in its danger. The truth is that the man you might call is almost certainly as starved as you are and would receive your reaching out not as neediness but as rescue. The pursuit that feels so humiliating to offer is precisely the gift every other man is secretly hoping to receive. But someone has to break the standoff. Someone has to be willing to look slightly foolish, to be the one who says the true thing first. And I would argue that the Christian man, of all men, should be the one to break it, because his whole faith is built on the scandal of admitted need.

What real friendship requires

There is a further difficulty, and it is worth naming, because even the men who manage to gather other men around them often stop short of actual friendship and settle for something thinner. They achieve proximity, they achieve activity, they find guys to do things with, and they call it friendship, but it is not, because the one ingredient that turns companionship into friendship is missing. That ingredient is disclosure. Two men can golf together for twenty years and know nothing true about each other, and many do.

Real friendship requires that a man let himself be known, that he say out loud the things he actually struggles with, that he stop performing the competent, untroubled version of himself and let another man see the real one. This is the wall that most male relationships never get over. Men will share opinions, share activities, share complaints about work and sports and the state of the world, and share almost nothing about their own interior. And so they remain, even in each other's regular company, fundamentally alone, because you cannot be known by someone to whom you have never disclosed anything worth knowing.

The friendship that actually meets a man's need is the friendship in which he can say, I am afraid I am failing as a father, or my marriage is in trouble and I do not know what to do, or I have a struggle I have never told anyone. Those sentences are the doorway, and most men never walk through it, and so they have companions but not friends, and they wonder why the loneliness persists even when they are surrounded. The cure for male loneliness is not more men in the room. It is one man in the room to whom you have finally told the truth.

What the Scriptures assume and we ignore

The Scriptures simply assume that men will have deep friendships, and describe them without embarrassment, and our culture has lost the very category the Bible takes for granted. David and Jonathan loved each other with a love the text is not ashamed to call remarkable. Jesus, who needed nothing, chose to gather twelve men around him and to draw three of them closer still, and in the garden on the worst night he specifically wanted his friends near, and was grieved when they slept. If the Son of God, in his humanity, wanted his friends present in his agony, then the man who thinks he is above needing friends has misunderstood not only friendship but manhood itself.

Here is what I have come to believe, having watched too many men, including men I love, drift into an isolation that eventually curdled into something darker. The male friendship crisis is not soft, and it is not optional, and it is not a lifestyle preference. It sits underneath a great deal of what we call the crisis of men. The isolated man is the man most vulnerable to despair, to addiction, to the slow rotting of the soul that has no one to be truthful with. When a man goes down, the people around him so often say afterward that they had no idea, that he seemed fine, that he never said a word. Of course he never said a word. He had no one to say it to. He had acquaintances. He needed a friend.

Building it on purpose

Because friendship no longer assembles itself through proximity the way it did in youth, it now has to be built on purpose, and this is where most men fail, not for lack of desire but for lack of structure. The men who actually have deep friendships in adulthood are almost always the men who built some structure to hold them, some recurring, defended, non negotiable rhythm that does not depend on anyone feeling like it in the moment. Friendship left to spontaneity in a busy adult life simply does not happen, because something more urgent always intrudes, and the friendship that everyone wanted quietly starves for lack of a time and a place.

So the practical answer is a rhythm. The same men, the same time, the same regularity, protected from the endless erosion of more urgent things. It might be a weekly breakfast, a standing evening, a monthly gathering, the particular shape matters less than the fact that it recurs and that the men have agreed to defend it. Within that structure, over months and years, the disclosure that turns companionship into friendship has room to happen, because the men are no longer strangers passing through each other's lives but a fixed company who keep showing up, and the trust that real friendship requires is built precisely by that showing up, again and again, until saying the true thing finally feels safe.

Adult friendship does not happen by accident anymore. It happens on purpose, on a schedule, defended against everything more urgent, or it does not happen at all.

The church should be, of all places, the natural home of this kind of friendship, and it is a rebuke to us that it so often is not. We gather men in the same room week after week and then let them leave as strangers, having shared a service but nothing of their actual lives, and we call it fellowship when it is merely attendance. A church that took the friendship crisis seriously would build the structures that let men actually know each other, would create the rooms and the rhythms in which disclosure could happen, would refuse to let men sit near each other for years while remaining fundamentally alone. The early church shared their lives, their homes, their struggles, their possessions, and we have shrunk that down to a shared hour on Sunday and wondered why our men are lonely.

This is unromantic, and something in us resists it, as though scheduling friendship robbed it of its warmth. But the warmth comes, and it comes precisely because the structure held long enough for it to grow. The alternative, waiting for friendship to happen spontaneously the way it did when we were young, is simply a decision to remain alone, because the conditions that once made it spontaneous are gone and are not coming back. The man who accepts this, who is willing to build the unglamorous structure and then defend it, is the man who will not be found, twenty years from now, sitting alone in a crowd wondering where all his friends went.

So I would press this on every man reading, and I press it on myself, a pastor surrounded by people and still capable of going relationally hungry in a crowd. Do not wait to be pursued. Be the one who pursues. Pick up the phone and call the man you keep meaning to call. Say the awkward true thing. Suggest the standing time together and then defend it against every more urgent demand. The friendships will not reassemble themselves. Someone has to pay the cost that no one warned us about. Let it be you.

chapters.title: Men and Emotional Health
chapters.summary: Most men were trained to feel exactly one emotion in public, and it was not sadness or fear. The cost of that training is showing up in our marriages, our bodies, and our sons.
chapters.body:
Ask most men how they are, and you will get one word. Fine. It is not that the man is hiding something in that moment, though sometimes he is. It is that the machinery for reporting anything more precise than fine was never installed. He was raised in a world that gave him a rich vocabulary for accomplishment and almost none for interior life, and so when you reach inside to find out what is actually happening, he finds a room with the lights off and no map.

I want to talk about the emotional health of men, and I want to do it without the therapeutic vocabulary that makes so many men close the door before the conversation starts. Because there is a real problem here, and it is killing us, sometimes literally, and the church has too often been silent about it or, worse, has spiritualized it into something a man cannot admit without feeling like a failure of faith.

The one permitted emotion

Here is the strange thing about how men are formed. We are not taught to have no emotions. We are taught to route every emotion through one acceptable channel. A boy learns early which feelings are allowed out of the house and which must stay locked in the basement. Sadness is not allowed, because sadness looks like weakness. Fear is not allowed, for the same reason. Loneliness is certainly not allowed, because a man who admits he is lonely has admitted he needs something, and needing is the cardinal sin of the code.

But one emotion is permitted, and so everything else gets converted into it. That emotion is anger. Anger is allowed because anger looks like strength, and so the sad man comes out angry, and the frightened man comes out angry, and the ashamed man comes out angry, and the lonely man comes out angry, and everyone around him thinks he is an angry man when in fact he is a grieving man who was only ever handed one tool. I have watched this in myself. I have snapped at my sons over something trivial and known, even as I did it, that the anger was a cover, that underneath it was fear about something else entirely, and that they were receiving the anger while the real thing stayed hidden even from me.

A man raised to convert every feeling into anger is not an angry man. He is a man in pain who was given a single language.

What the numb man cannot do

The cost of this training is not mainly that the man is unhappy, though he often is. The cost is that a man who cannot feel his own interior cannot be present to anyone else's. Emotional numbness is not a private condition. It leaks into every relationship the man has.

His wife tells him she feels alone in the marriage, and he genuinely does not understand, because he has been physically present the whole time. He has provided, he has been faithful, he has done the things. What he has not done is be emotionally available, because he does not have access to his own emotional life, and you cannot offer someone access to a room you cannot enter yourself. So she feels married to a competent stranger, and he feels unjustly accused, and neither of them can name the actual problem, which is that somewhere around age nine he learned to lock the basement and he never found the key again.

His children get the same locked door. A father who cannot say I am afraid cannot teach a son what to do with fear except to hide it. A father who cannot grieve openly raises children who think grief is shameful. The numbness is not neutral. It reproduces. And so the wound goes down the generations, each father handing his sons the same single tool and the same locked basement, and everyone calling it strength.

The lie that faith should have fixed it

The church has a particular way of making this worse, and I have been guilty of it from the pulpit. We take a real emotional struggle and we spiritualize it in a way that shames the man out of naming it. A man is depressed, and we tell him to have more joy in the Lord, as though depression were a failure of gratitude. A man is anxious, and we quote him the verse about being anxious for nothing, as though the command dissolved the condition. A man is grieving, and we rush him toward the resurrection before he has been allowed to sit in the tomb where his Savior once lay.

We hand a drowning man a Bible verse and are surprised when he stops telling us he is drowning.

This is pastoral malpractice, and it drives the struggle underground, which is the last place we should want it. The man learns that his church is not a safe place to be a real person, and so he performs wellness on Sunday and falls apart alone on Tuesday, and we congratulate ourselves that our men are doing so well. Meanwhile the Scriptures we are misusing are full of men who did the opposite of what we demand. David screamed at God in the Psalms. Elijah asked to die. Job cursed the day he was born and God did not rebuke him for it. Jesus himself sweat blood and begged for the cup to pass and cried out that he had been forsaken. Our tradition has more room for male emotion than our churches do.

The body keeps the account

What we do not say often enough is that the suppressed interior does not simply disappear. It goes somewhere. A feeling that is not allowed out through the front door of awareness will find a back door, and in men that back door is very often the body. The stress that is never named becomes the clenched jaw, the tight chest, the sleeplessness, the drinking that starts a little earlier each year, the low grade physical toll of a man carrying a weight he will not admit he is carrying. Men die younger than women for many reasons, and some of them are biological, but some of them are this. A man can only pretend he feels nothing for so long before the pretending costs him his health.

I have known men who prided themselves on their unflappability, who were never rattled, who handled every crisis with the same flat calm, and who were, underneath that calm, quietly falling apart in ways their bodies knew before their minds would admit. The calm was not health. It was dissociation dressed as strength. A man who has genuinely made peace with a hard thing looks different from a man who has simply stopped letting himself feel it, though from the outside they can resemble each other, and the second man will often be praised for the very numbness that is killing him.

This is why emotional health is not a soft, optional, therapeutic add on to a man's real life. It is closer to the foundation of everything. A man who cannot access his own interior cannot know himself, and a man who does not know himself is at the mercy of forces inside him that he cannot see and therefore cannot govern. He will be driven by fears he will not name, wounded by griefs he will not feel, and controlled by an anger whose true source he has never once examined. The examined interior is not self indulgence. It is the precondition of self government, and self government is the precondition of leading anyone or anything well.

Naming as the first act of health

So what is the way forward, practically, for a man who recognizes himself in this and does not want to hand the locked basement to his sons. It begins, unglamorously, with naming. The single most healing act available to a numb man is to learn to name what he actually feels, in words more precise than fine and more honest than angry.

This sounds small. It is not. When a man learns to catch himself mid anger and ask what is actually underneath this, when he learns to say to himself, I am not angry, I am afraid, or I am not irritated, I am ashamed, something begins to shift. The naming does not fix the feeling, but it changes his relationship to it. The feeling is no longer driving the car from the trunk. It has been brought into the front seat where it can be dealt with. This is not weakness. It is the beginning of self government, and a man who cannot govern his own interior cannot lead anything worth leading.

And it requires other men. A man cannot do this repair alone, because the whole wound was formed in isolation and it can only be healed in the presence of another. He needs at least one man, and preferably a few, to whom he can say the true thing without watching their faces to see if they now think less of him. The absence of this kind of friendship among men is itself a crisis, one large enough for its own conversation. But it begins here, with the recognition that the fine is a lie, that the anger is a cover, that the basement can be opened, and that the God who made us with these interiors did not intend for half the human race to spend its life pretending the interiors are not there.

The false choice we have handed men

Part of why men resist this work is that we have handed them a false choice, and both options are bad. On one side is the old model, the man of stone, unfeeling and impenetrable, strong in the sense of being unreachable. On the other side is a caricature of the emotional man, the one who is all feeling and no spine, who processes everything and does nothing, whose interior life has swallowed his capacity to act. Men look at those two options and understandably choose the stone, because at least the stone can function, at least the stone can lead, at least the stone is not the soft, self absorbed figure they have been taught to despise.

But that is a false choice, and it has trapped a generation of men in a needless dilemma. The goal is not to trade strength for feeling, or feeling for strength. The goal is a man who has both, who feels deeply and acts decisively, whose access to his own interior makes him more capable rather than less, more present, more wise, more able to lead because he actually understands what is happening inside himself and inside the people he is leading. Emotional health is not the opposite of strength. It is a component of the highest strength, the strength that comes from a man who is not secretly at the mercy of forces he refuses to examine.

The choice was never between the man of stone and the man of endless feeling. The mature man feels everything and still acts. That is the harder thing, and the stronger.

There is a spiritual dimension to all of this that the therapeutic frame alone cannot reach, and it is worth naming as we close. The man who cannot feel his own interior is cut off not only from himself and from other people but, in a quiet way, from God, because so much of the life with God happens through the very faculties he has shut down. He cannot bring his grief to God if he will not feel his grief. He cannot know the comfort of God in his fear if he refuses to admit the fear. He cannot experience being loved by God if he has amputated the capacity to be moved. Emotional numbness is not spiritually neutral. It walls a man off from the God who meets us precisely in the places we are most tempted to keep sealed.

Think again of Jesus, who is the pattern for everything. He was not a man of stone. He wept, he grieved, he was moved in his gut with compassion, he agonized in a garden and let his friends see it. And he was not a man drowned in his own feeling, paralyzed and self absorbed. He felt everything the garden held and still rose and walked toward the cross. That is the integration we are after, and it is not soft, and it is not weak, and it is available to any man willing to do the slow, humbling work of learning to enter the interior he was taught to keep locked. The stone man cannot do what Jesus did, because the stone cannot feel the cup he is choosing to drink. Only the man who feels it can truly choose it.

I am still learning this. I lead a church and I raise sons and I have preached these very words, and I still catch myself, decades in, giving the world my one permitted emotion when something truer is waiting underneath. But I catch it faster now. And when I do, I try to name it, first to God and then, harder, to the people I love. That is not a therapy technique. It is honesty, and honesty is the only ground the Spirit can heal on.

chapters.title: Pornography, Shame, and the Way Out
chapters.summary: The strategies most men use against pornography are built on the very shame that keeps them enslaved. The way out is not more willpower or more secrecy. It runs in the exact opposite direction.
chapters.body:
I am going to write plainly about something the church prefers to handle at arm's length, because the arm's length approach has failed an entire generation of men and I am tired of watching it fail them. Pornography is not a marginal problem in the pews. It is close to universal among men under a certain age, and it is common enough among older men that no one should feel singled out by an honest sermon. If we cannot speak about it directly, we have no business pretending we are discipling men at all.

But I do not want to add to the noise. There is already a great deal of writing on this, and much of it, even the well meant Christian writing, is quietly making the problem worse. It is making it worse because it is built on shame, and shame is not the cure for this. Shame is the engine of it. That is the thing I most need a man caught in this to understand, so let me build to it carefully.

The cycle everyone knows and no one names

Let me describe the cycle, because every man caught in it recognizes it and almost no one has had it described back to them, and there is relief simply in being seen. It goes like this. A man feels something, usually not lust at all but stress, or loneliness, or boredom, or a low grinding sense of inadequacy. He does not have language for the feeling and he does not have another way to soothe it. So he reaches for the thing that reliably delivers a few minutes of relief. For a moment the ache is quiet.

Then the shame arrives, and it is enormous, out of all proportion, and it tells him he is disgusting, that he is a hypocrite, that if anyone knew they would be finished with him, that he has done this a thousand times and will never be free. The shame is unbearable. And what does a man do with an unbearable feeling he has no other way to soothe. He reaches for the thing that soothes. The shame becomes the stress that drives the next episode. The cure the church prescribes, feel worse about it, is fuel poured on the fire it is trying to put out.

Shame does not break the cycle. Shame is the cycle. It is the fuel dressed up as the cure.

Why willpower is the wrong weapon

The first strategy most men try is willpower, and it is doomed, and it is important to understand why so the man stops blaming his own weakness. Willpower is doomed because this behavior is not primarily a lust problem. It is a coping problem. The man is not mainly seeking pleasure. He is medicating pain, and the pornography is simply the anesthetic he happened to find.

You cannot willpower your way out of a medication when you have not addressed the pain it is medicating. Take away the anesthetic by force and the pain is still there, screaming, and the man white knuckles for a few days or a few weeks and then the pain wins, because pain always wins against willpower over the long run. Then he concludes he is uniquely broken, uniquely weak, uniquely unable to want God more than this. And that conclusion is another dose of shame, which is another log on the fire.

The question that actually matters is not how do I stop wanting this. The question is what is the pain I am medicating, and is there anywhere else to bring it. Until a man asks that question, every promise he makes to himself is a promise made by the part of him that is not in charge in the moment of reaching.

The way out runs through the light

Here is the counterintuitive heart of it. The thing that keeps a man enslaved is not mainly the behavior. It is the secrecy. The behavior could not survive contact with the light, and so it demands the dark, and as long as the man keeps it in the dark it retains all its power. Everything about this sin depends on no one knowing. So the way out begins with the single most terrifying and most healing act available to him, which is to tell someone the truth.

Not to confess to God only. He has been confessing to God for years, alone, in the same dark that hides the behavior, and it has not set him free, because the secrecy is intact. God already knows and has already forgiven, and the confession to God, while real, does not break the isolation that the sin feeds on. He has to say it out loud to a human being who can see his face. He has to let one trusted man know the specific truth. And in that moment, the sin loses the darkness it requires to live.
